History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with 3-week history of progressive left-sided hearing difficulty, constant left facial/jaw numbness, intermittent left-ear tinnitus and occasional dizziness; clinician suspects Bell’s palsy and arranged same-day in-person neurological/ear examination.

History:
• Presenting complaints: Reduced hearing and numbness on left side of face.  
• Onset/duration: Began ~3 weeks ago; gradual progression.  
• Laterality: Entirely left-sided (ear and adjacent jawline).  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the left ear.  
  – Occasional dizziness coinciding with tinnitus.  
• Pertinent negatives: No limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, visual changes, ear discharge, ear pain, ear itch, fever, recent trauma.  
• Current status: Facial numbness present at time of consult; hearing still reduced.  
• ROS otherwise non-contributory based on transcript.

Past Medical History:
• Nasal polyps – treated intermittently with intranasal spray (name and dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Remote episode labelled “labyrinthitis” – no ongoing symptoms.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• Intranasal spray for nasal polyps – prn, name/dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Rennie (OTC antacid) – prn, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No other medications.

Allergies:
• Latex (reaction not specified).

Social History:
• Occupation: Professional jockey; training reduced due to current symptoms.  
• Living situation: Lives with partner.  
• Pets: None.  
• Tobacco, alcohol, recreational drugs: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Brother with neurofibromatosis (type unspecified).  
• No other familial illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
• No vital signs or in-office examination performed (video consultation).  
• No cranial nerve, otoscopic, or neurological findings documented.

Investigations:
• None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Left-sided hearing loss, facial numbness, intermittent tinnitus/dizziness  
  • Assessment: Unilateral cranial-nerve–related symptoms; clinician’s provisional diagnosis is Bell’s palsy. Differential includes vestibular schwannoma and other cranial-nerve pathologies.  
  • Plan:  
    – Arrange same-day face-to-face appointment for comprehensive neurological examination and otoscopic evaluation (booking via clinic support team).  
    – Reassure patient that condition not believed to be life-threatening.  
    – Further management (e.g., imaging, audiology) to be determined after in-person assessment.

Issue 2 – Health-related anxiety about potential serious illness  
  • Assessment: Patient expressed fear of life-threatening condition.  
  • Plan: Provided verbal reassurance; will reinforce after definitive examination.

Issue 3 – Chronic nasal polyps  
  • Assessment: Stable; managed with prn nasal spray.  
  • Plan: Continue current intranasal therapy as needed; no changes today.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) – Likelihood: High  
   • Progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial numbness; family history of neurofibromatosis increases risk.
2. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – Likelihood: Moderate  
   • Fits unilateral facial sensory change; clinician’s working diagnosis, though absence of motor weakness is atypical.
3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome – Likelihood: Low-Moderate  
   • Could explain unilateral auditory and facial symptoms but pain and rash are absent (opposing evidence).

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but expected elements: Vital signs, full medication list with doses, comprehensive allergies (reaction details), smoking/alcohol history, physical exam findings.  
● Conflicts: DDx ranks vestibular schwannoma as most likely, whereas clinician leans toward Bell’s palsy (conflict noted but both documented).  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional interruptions but clinically adequate information captured.
